title: Influence Dynamics and Stagewise Data Attribution
claim: Regular models develop by smooth, monotonic posterior concentration, while singular models develop in stages with phase transitions, so attribution must be stagewise.
layout: 2 panels side-by-side, each with loss curve and posterior-over-n diagram; phase-transition label
description: Two side-by-side panels contrast regular and stagewise development. Panel (a), labeled Regular Development (Bernstein von-Mises), shows a single-basin loss curve with a quadratic dotted approximation and the MLE w*. Beside it is a diagram with an axis for w* and a sample-count arrow n. Dotted funnel lines narrow as n grows, and three posterior densities p(w|D_n) get steadily sharper. Panel (b), labeled Stagewise Development (Watanabe), shows a double-well loss curve with a broad minimum u* and a sharp, narrow minimum v*. Its n-axis diagram has two arrows, u* and v*, and a marked critical n*. Three posteriors are shown: a broad one, a bimodal one with a curved arrow marked Phase transition, and a sharp one. The figure is black and white line art with gray-filled densities, and the eye goes first to the contrasting curves.
caption: Stagewise learning requires stagewise data attribution. (a) In regular models, development is a uniform, monotonic process of posterior concentration around a single solution (Bernstein--von Mises). (b) In singular models, development is a stagewise process where the posterior undergoes phase transitions (Watanabe's singular learning theory). This stagewise development means the influence one sample has on another can profoundly change over the course of the learning process.
abstract: Current training data attribution (TDA) methods treat the influence one sample has on another as static, but neural networks learn in distinct stages that exhibit changing patterns of influence. In this work, we introduce a framework for stagewise data attribution grounded in singular learning theory. We predict that influence can change non-monotonically, including sign flips and sharp peaks at developmental transitions. We first validate these predictions analytically and empirically in a toy model, showing that dynamic shifts in influence directly map to the model's progressive learning of a semantic hierarchy. Finally, we demonstrate these phenomena at scale in language models, where token-level influence changes align with known developmental stages.
